prompt: A model scores 99% on training data but 60% on new data.
tells: 99% on training data but 60% on new data
why: The model does brilliantly on data it trained on and poorly on new data. That gap means it learned the training set too closely: overfitting.

prompt: The model memorized the training examples, including their noise.
why: Memorizing the training examples, noise and all, means it won't generalize to new ones. That's overfitting.

prompt: A very deep decision tree has a separate branch for almost every training row.
tells: a separate branch for almost every training row
why: A branch for nearly every training row means the tree has memorized the data rather than learning general rules. Too much complexity overfits.

prompt: Like a student who memorizes practice answers and fails when the questions change.
why: Memorizing practice answers works only until the questions change. A model that memorizes its training data fails on new data the same way: overfitting.
trap: The new questions are the test; the failure is overfitting.

prompt: Adding more and more features makes training accuracy rise while test accuracy drops.
why: Training accuracy goes up while test accuracy goes down, so the extra features help it memorize, not generalize. That's overfitting.
trap: Rising training accuracy rules out underfitting.

prompt: The fitted curve wiggles through every training point exactly.
why: Passing exactly through every training point means the curve is fitting the random noise too. That's overfitting.
trap: It's a regression, but the problem is overfitting.
